READING 43
INTRODUCTION TO EQUITY
VALUATION
MODULE 43.1: MEASURES AND MODELS OF
EQUITY VALUE
LOS 43.a: Contrast price and value for an equity security.
Intrinsic value or fundamental value is the rational value investors would
place on a stock if they had full knowledge of its characteristics. Unlike its
market price, a stock’s intrinsic value is not directly observable. Analysts use
valuation models to estimate the intrinsic values of stocks.
Individual investors, based on their assumptions about the future, arrive at their
own perceived value for a stock. Market prices incorporate perceived values of
active market participants. If an investor’s perceived value is higher than the
current market price, the investor considers the stock undervalued by the market;
if the investor’s perceived value is lower than the stock’s market price, the
investor believes the stock is overvalued by the market. If the perceived value
equals the market price, the investor views the stock as fairly valued. Investors
will tend to sell or reduce the portfolio weights of stocks they perceive to be
overvalued and buy or increase the portfolio weights of stocks they see as
undervalued.
Investors use the following three approaches to determine perceived value:
Naïve or story-based valuation is an informal approach that does not link
valuation to company finances or fundamentals. Investors often use naïve or
story-based valuation for meme stocks that derive their (baseless) value from
social media activity, or cult companies that have a dedicated following of the
company’s founders or products.

Relative valuation relies on comparing a company’s fundamentals to a peer
group of similar companies. Relative valuation is based on the idea that
companies with similar characteristics should trade at similar price multiples.
Absolute or fundamental valuation evaluates a company based on only its own
characteristics and fundamentals, without regard to a benchmark. One
fundamental approach is to value the stock as the present value of future cash
flows available to the investor, discounted at an appropriate risk-adjusted
discount rate.
Analysts often estimate a stock’s intrinsic value as a range rather than a specific
price. A stock’s recent low and high prices determine its market price range.
Intrinsic value ranges are derived from different estimates of inputs into an
analyst’s valuation model, or they are based on value estimates from different
models. Graphically, we can visualize a side-by-side representation of these
ranges in a floating bar valuation chart, as shown in Figure 43.1.
Figure 43.1: Floating Bar Valuation for XYZ, Inc.
A scenario analysis estimates a base case value for a stock as well as a bullish
(more favorable) and a bearish (less favorable) case value. The analyst’s
expected value for the stock is then a probability-weighted average of these
estimated values.
LOS 43.b: Contrast the use of book value of equity, market capitalization,
and enterprise value as indicators of intrinsic value.
Book Value of Equity
The book value of equity is the value of the firm’s assets on the balance sheet
minus its liabilities and minority interest. It increases when the firm has positive

net income and retained earnings that flow into shareholders’ equity. When
management makes decisions that increase income and retained earnings, they
increase the book value of equity.
Analysts often evaluate book value of equity on a per-share basis. Book value
per share (BVPS) is the book value of equity divided by the number of shares
outstanding.
Assets of the firm can be tangible (e.g., equipment and inventory) or intangible
(e.g., patents, copyrights, and balance sheet goodwill). The book value of
tangible property on the balance sheet depends on how recently it was acquired
and on the depreciation method chosen for long-lived assets. Intangible property
that is internally generated is usually expensed, so it does not appear on the
balance sheet. Purchased intangible assets are amortized over their useful lives
or subject to impairment testing. Recall from Financial Statement Analysis that
goodwill arises when one firm acquires another at a price exceeding the acquired
firm’s fair value of net identifiable assets.
Differences in accounting methods across companies affect their assets’ balance
sheet carrying values and, hence, their BVPS.
As a valuation metric, book value is more appropriate for firms with substantial
tangible assets. It is less appropriate for early-stage firms whose balance sheet
values do not reflect future earnings potential, or for firms with significant
intangible assets.
Another approach to estimating book value is to add the components of
stockholders’ equity, excluding minority or noncontrolling interest:

Apoka Pharmaceuticals:

Apoka has 500,000 shares outstanding. Calculate Apoka’s book value and
book value per share.
Answer:
A company has a negative book value of equity if its assets are less than its
liabilities. This is often the case with firms that are in financial distress or
bankruptcy. However, a negative book value can also occur with profitable and
valuable companies, such as those in a rapid growth stage or companies that
have an aggressive stock buyback program. Repurchases of stock increase
treasury stock (which is a negative value within stockholders’ equity); thus, they
may turn the book value negative.
Market Capitalization
Market capitalization is the total value of a firm’s outstanding equity shares
based on market prices and reflects investors’ expectations about the firm’s
future performance.
market capitalization = share price × number of shares outstanding
While book value is based on balance sheet carrying values (e.g., depreciated
cost for tangible long-lived assets), market capitalization reflects the fair value of
assets. Further, market capitalization is based on a company’s value as a going
concern, as opposed to the prospect of selling its assets piecemeal. In other

words, market capitalization includes value attributable to investor expectations
about a company’s future earnings.
When market capitalization is higher than book value, we may consider the
difference to be excess value that the firm is creating through its operations. If
market capitalization is lower than book value, an analyst should investigate the
shortfall to determine whether it represents an undervalued stock or an
uncompetitive company.
A relative valuation metric used by analysts is the price-to-book ratio (P/B):
P/B = market price of stock / BVPS
      = market capitalization / book value
Firms with excess value have a P/B greater than one, and firms with a value
shortfall have a P/B less than one.
P/B is used as a metric for valuation relative to a benchmark, such as the average
P/B of a peer group. Assuming similar characteristics, a firm’s P/B should be
close to the benchmark. Absent justifiable reasons, if a stock trades at a P/B
significantly higher than the benchmark, the stock would be considered
relatively overvalued; and if it trades at a P/B significantly lower than its
benchmark, the stock is relatively undervalued.

Enterprise Value
Enterprise value (EV) measures total company value. EV represents the cost to
acquire a firm.
EV = market value of common and preferred stock + net debt
EV = market value of common and preferred stock + market value of debt − cash and short-term
investments
Net debt is the market value of a company’s debt minus its cash and short-term
investments. Cash and short-term investments are subtracted because an
acquirer’s cost for a firm would be decreased by the amount of the target’s liquid
assets. Although an acquirer assumes the firm’s debt, it also receives the firm’s
cash and short-term investments.
EV is appropriate when an analyst wants to compare the values of firms that
have significant differences in capital structure. If the companies are located in
different countries, an analyst must convert their EVs into a common currency
before comparing them.
EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization have
been subtracted) is commonly used as the denominator for EV multiples (EBIT
or revenue can also be used).
EXAMPLE: Calculating EV/EBITDA multiples

Daniel, Inc., is a manufacturer of small refrigerators and other appliances. The
following figures are from Daniel’s most recent financial statements except for
the market value of long-term debt, which has been estimated from financial
market data.
Calculate the EV/EBITDA multiple.
Answer:
First, we must estimate the market value of the firm’s short-term debt and
liabilities. To do so, subtract the book value of long-term debt from the book
value of total debt: $2,100,000 − $900,000 = $1,200,000. This is the book
value of the firm’s short-term debt. If we assume the company is not in
financial distress, the market value of these short-term items should be close to
their book value. (As we will see in the Fixed Income topic area, the market
values of debt instruments approach their face values as they get close to
maturity.)
Add the market value of long-term debt to get the market value of total debt:
$600,000 + $1,200,000 = $1,800,000.
The market value of equity is the stock price multiplied by the number of
shares: $40 × 200,000 = $8,000,000.
The EV of the firm is the sum of debt and equity minus cash: $1,800,000 +
$8,000,000 − $250,000 = $9,550,000. So, EV/EBITDA = $9,550,000 /
$1,000,000 ≈ 9.6.
If the competitor or industry average EV/EBITDA is above 9.6, Daniel is
relatively undervalued. If the competitor or industry average EV/EBITDA is
below 9.6, Daniel is relatively overvalued.
LOS 43.c: Describe major categories of equity valuation models and explain
their advantages and disadvantages.

Analysts use various models to estimate the value of equities. Usually, an analyst
will use more than one model with several different sets of inputs to determine a
range of possible stock values. The two basic approaches to valuation are
absolute valuation and relative valuation.
Absolute Valuation Approaches
Absolute valuation uses only company-specific information. Two absolute
valuation models are present value models and an asset-based approach.
In present value models or discounted cash flow models, a stock’s value is
estimated as the present value of cash distributed to shareholders (dividend
discount models) or the present value of cash available to shareholders after the
firm meets its necessary capital expenditures and working capital expenses (free
cash flow to equity models). Alternatively, valuation of the whole firm (value of
equity plus value of debt) is calculated as the present value of free cash flow to
the firm.
Another discounted cash flow approach is based on residual income valuation,
where the current book value is added to the present value of future residual
income. Residual income is net income less an equity charge that is based on the
book value at the beginning of the year.
The discount rate used for dividend, FCFE, and residual income models is the
required return on equity, while the discount rate for FCFF models is the
weighted average cost of capital.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
In our next readings, we will examine all these models in detail.
While present value models are based on sound fundamental theory, the value
estimates are highly sensitive to the estimates of their inputs. For mature firms
with stable and predictable dividend policies, using dividend discount models
makes sense. FCFE models are appropriate for non-dividend-paying firms with
stable capital structures. When a firm has a negative FCFE or when the capital
structure is not stable (e.g., high reliance on debt or significant stock
repurchases), FCFF models are more appropriate. Residual income models are
useful for firms that do not pay dividends or have negative free cash flow.
Advantages of discounted cash flow models are as follows:

They are based on the fundamental concept of discounted present value and are
well grounded in finance theory.
They allow analysts to change assumptions, such as revenue growth and
margins, to evaluate their impact on valuation.
Disadvantages are as follows:
Inputs must be estimated.
Value estimates are highly sensitive to input values.
The second type of absolute valuation approach is an asset-based model. In an
asset-based model, an analyst estimates the intrinsic value of a company’s
common stock as the company’s assets minus its liabilities and preferred stock.
Analysts typically adjust the book values of the assets and liabilities to their fair
values.
Asset-based models are suitable for companies with assets whose market values
are readily available. For example, with resource-rich firms (e.g., mining
companies with known proven deposits), the value of the firm’s assets can be
determined readily. Some firms may have real estate holdings with values that
exceed their cash flow generating potential, and an asset-based valuation would
need to incorporate that information.
Advantages of asset-based models are as follows:
They can provide floor values for a stock or a company.
They are useful for valuing divisions that are being sold or liquidated.
They are most reliable when the firm has primarily tangible short-term assets,
assets with ready market values, or when the firm is being liquidated.
They are increasingly useful for valuing public firms that report fair values of
assets.
Disadvantages are as follows:
They do not value the firm as a going concern, so they ignore margins, the
efficient use of assets, and the competitive landscape.
They ignore effects of taxes.
Relative Valuation Approaches
Two basic types of relative valuation models (or multiplier models) can be
used to estimate intrinsic values. The first type values a company from the

perspective of equity owners. The ratio of stock price to fundamentals such as
earnings, sales, book value, or cash flow per share is used to determine whether
a stock is fairly valued. For example, many analysts use the price-to-earnings
ratio (P/E). A trailing P/E ratio uses past EPS, while a leading P/E ratio uses
forecast EPS for the next year. Analysts routinely adjust companies’ reported
earnings to exclude nonrecurring or extraordinary items. If EPS is negative or
very low, this multiple loses its usefulness.
EXAMPLE: Method of comparables
MK Technologies shares are selling for $50. Earnings for the last 12 months
were $2 per share. The average trailing P/E for firms in MK’s industry is 32
times. Determine whether MK is overvalued or undervalued using the method
of comparables.
Answer:
MK is relatively undervalued because its observed trailing P/E (25 times) is
less than the industry average trailing P/E (32 times).
The second type of relative valuation model, which measures value from the
perspectives of both equity and debt investors, is based on the ratio of EV to
either EBITDA, EBIT, or revenue. As with other comparables-based models,
values of an EV multiple that differ significantly from their benchmark may
suggest overvaluation or undervaluation, unless they are justified by firm-
specific attributes.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
We will examine both of these comparables-based approaches to
valuation in our next readings.
Analysts often use multiple methods to estimate value, which may result in
inconsistencies in valuations. A weighted average can be used to arrive at the
value estimate, with higher weights for models in which the analyst has greater
confidence in input estimates. Analysts should also examine the consistency of
assumptions used in various approaches to reconcile significant valuation
differences.
MODULE QUIZ 43.1

1. Alcott Sidney is a tech influencer with a loyal fan base. Sidney started SMX Company,
and its first product is a browser with integrated social media. Fans have purchased stock
in SMX, and it is currently trading at a P/E multiple three times those of comparable
companies. SMX stock is most accurately described as:
A. undervalued.
B. a meme stock.
C. a cult stock.
2. Alpha Semiconductors is a growing company that uses large amounts of debt to
repurchase its stock. Alpha’s dividend payout ratio varies from year to year. Which
measure of future cash flows would be most appropriate to use in present value models
to value Alpha stock?
A. Free cash flow to equity.
B. Free cash flow to the firm.
C. Dividends.
3. Beta Consumer Products Limited has a dominant market position in several consumer
products. Beta has a stable revenue stream and pays 80% of its earnings in dividends.
Which measure of future cash flows is most appropriate to use in present value models to
value Beta stock?
A. Free cash flow to equity.
B. Free cash flow to the firm.
C. Dividends.
4. Spills, Inc., has 250,000 shares outstanding. Spills stock trades at a price of €15, while its
book value per share is €16. Based only on this information, it is most appropriate to
conclude that Spills has:
A. a value shortfall.
B. excess value.
C. an undervalued stock.
5. Valley Company has announced that it will cease operating and liquidate within a year. An
analyst who wants to determine the value of Valley’s equity shares should most
appropriately use a(n):
A. asset-based model.
B. relative valuation model.
C. discounted cash flow model.
KEY CONCEPTS
LOS 43.a
Intrinsic value is the rational value investors would place on a stock if they had
full knowledge of the company’s characteristics. Perceived value varies based on
the assumptions used by different investors and can be based on naïve or story-
based valuation, relative valuation, or absolute valuation.
LOS 43.b

Book value of equity is the value of a firm’s balance sheet assets minus its
liabilities and minority interest. Book value per share is book value divided by
the number of outstanding shares.
Market capitalization is the current market price of a firm’s stock multiplied by
the number of outstanding shares. When market capitalization exceeds (falls
short of) book value, the firm is generating excess value (a value shortfall)
attributable to its ability to generate future cash flows.
Enterprise value (EV) is the market value of common and preferred stock, plus
the market value of debt, minus cash and short-term investments. The ratio of
EV to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA)
is frequently used for relative valuation.
LOS 43.c
Absolute valuation models include present value (discounted cash flow) models
based on future dividends, free cash flow, or residual income; and asset-based
models based on the fair value of a company’s assets minus its liabilities and
preferred stock.
Relative valuation models based on multiples such as price-to-earnings, price-to-
book value, and EV-to-EBITDA are used to value a company relative to its
peers.
ANSWER KEY FOR MODULE QUIZ
Module Quiz 43.1
. C SMX stock is best characterized as a cult stock because its valuation results
from a loyal following of the company’s founder. (LOS 43.a)
. B Because the company’s capital structure is volatile (using debt to repurchase
stock), FCFF would be preferred over FCFE, and dividend-based present
value models are not appropriate for companies with low or volatile
dividend payments. (LOS 43.b)
. C Dividend discount models are appropriate for companies with stable and
predictable dividend payments. (LOS 43.b)
. A Companies with a lower share price than their book value per share are
considered to have a value shortfall. An analyst should investigate the

reason for a value shortfall before concluding that the stock is undervalued.
(LOS 43.b)
. A Asset-based models can be applied to firms that are expected to cease
operating. Other valuation techniques are more appropriate for evaluating
going concerns. (LOS 43.c)
